### Microscopy

Worms were mounted for all live imaging studies using our auxin-inducible conditional paralysis method, which is described in Cahoon and Libuda, 2021. Briefly, young adult worms (18–24 hr post L4) from a parental generation that was grown on NGM with either 1 mM auxin (for oocyte studies) or 10 mM auxin (for spermatocyte studies) were picked into 1 µL drop of live imaging media (M9 media with 25 mM serotonin [Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# H7752, Rog and Dernburg, 2015], 0.08% tricaine [ethyl 3-aminobenzoate methanesulfonate; Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# E10521-50G], 0.008% tetramisole hydrochloride [Sigma-Aldrich, Cat# T1512-10G]) and either 1 mM or 10 mM auxin (naphthaleneacetic acid [K-NAA], PhytoTechnology Laboratories, Cat# N610; Martinez et al., 2020) on a 22 × 40 mm (no. 1.5) coverslip. (Note: we found that poly-lysine treating the coverslips was not necessary for immobilization of the worms in most cases as long as the liquid under the agarose pad is minimal.) Also, 7–9% agarose pads (Invitrogen, Cat# 16500500) were gently placed over the top of the worms and excess liquid was wicked away using Whatman paper. A microscope slide was adhered to the agarose pad worm coverslip sandwich using a ring of Vaseline around the pad. Worms were then imaged using the setting described below. For both SC intensity and photobleaching studies, worms were imaged immediately following mounting and worms were only kept mounted for a max of 1 hr even though worms can survive being mounted for 2–3 hr (Cahoon and Libuda, 2021).

We did note that previous studies displayed higher fractions of SYP-3 recovery, which is likely caused by our studies not upshifting the worms to 25°C overnight (Nadarajan et al., 2017; Pattabiraman et al., 2017; Rog et al., 2017). Shifting the worms to 25°C is known to cause significant elevations in meiotic gene expression and is used to enhance expression of fluorescently tagged meiotic proteins (Pattabiraman et al., 2017; Song et al., 2010; Yokoo et al., 2012). Notably, we found that in recombination-deficient mutants, such as cosa-1, the elevated levels of GFP::SYP-2 protein in the SC with the elevation in protein expression that comes at 25°C caused large aggregates to form in mid/late pachytene that would persist into diakinesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). When the worms were only grown at 20°C without any 25°C upshift, these aggregates did not form. Thus, none of the worms for the studies in this paper were placed at 25°C overnight. Nevertheless, the trends appear the same for progressive stabilization with both GFP::SYP-3 and mCherry::SYP-3 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that mCherry and GFP fluorescent tags of SYP-3 do not appear to illicit differential dynamics (Nadarajan et al., 2017; Pattabiraman et al., 2017; Rog et al., 2017).

All live imaging studies of SYP-2::GFP, mCherry::SYP-3, SYP-5::GFP, and SYP-6::GFP were imaged on a Nikon CSU SoRa Spinning Disk Microscope with a ×60 water lens/N.A. 1.2 using a Z-step size of 0.3 µm. For SC intensity quantifications, the laser power and exposure times were kept consistent for all genotypes. All GFP::SYP-2, SYP-5::GFP, and SYP-6::GFP were imaged using the 488 laser at 16% power and 500 ms exposure time. All mCherry::SYP-3 imaging used the 561 laser at 25% power and 700 ms exposure time. Additionally, only the bottom half of the germline closest to the coverslip was imaged and germlines were not imaged if the position of the mounted worm caused the gut to cover germline or moved parts of the germline deeper into the worm.

The FRAP studies were performed as described in Pattabiraman et al., 2017 with minor changes. Briefly, a Z-stack was taken prior to photobleaching to obtain a pre-bleach image. Then, a region of interest defined by the point tool in Elements was photobleached. A timelapse was started immediately post-photobleaching with images captured every 5 min for 35 min to monitor the fluorescence recovery. Pilot experiments showed that the 35 min timepoint displayed the highest recovery fluorescence observed before the signal plateaued. So, to minimize photobleaching and phototoxicity effects, we concluded the recovery timelapses at 35 min. For photobleaching small regions of GFP::SYP-2 or mCherry::SYP-3, a 405 laser was used with 1–5% laser power and 10–30 ms exposure depending on the germline location of the nucleus and the tagged protein with GFP::SYP-2 requiring less laser power to photobleach than mCherry::SYP-3. Previous studies showed that immobilized worms without serotonin have significantly diminished or absent chromosome motion, and the loss of this motion does not impair SC recovery dynamics (Pattabiraman et al., 2017; Rog and Dernburg, 2015; Rog et al., 2017). Since the addition of chromosome motion makes the FRAP recovery analysis very challenging, we did not include serotonin to minimize the motion of the chromosomes and to allow for better tracking of the photobleached SC region within each nucleus during the recovery timelapse.

Immunofluorescence slides of fixed gonad were imaged on a GE DeltaVision microscope with a ×63/N.A. 1.42 lens and 1.5× optivar at 1024 × 1024 pixel dimensions. Images were acquired using 0.2 µm Z-step size and deconvolved with softWoRx deconvolution software.

### Immunohistochemisty

Immunofluorescence was performed as described in Cahoon and Libuda, 2021; Libuda et al., 2013. Briefly, gonads were dissected in egg buffer with 0.1% Tween20 onto VWR Superfrost Plus slides from 18 to 24 hr post L4 worms. Dissected gonads were fixed in 5% paraformaldehyde for 5 min, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and fixed for 1 min in 100% methanol at –20°C. Slides were washed three times in PBS + 0.1% Tween20 (PBST) for 5 min each and incubated in block (0.7% bovine serum albumin in PBST) for 1 hr. Primary antibodies (chicken anti-RAD-51, 1:1500 [Kurhanewicz et al., 2020; Toraason et al., 2021]; rabbit anti-SYP-1, 1:1000 [gift from Silva Lab]; rabbit anti-DSB-2 [Rosu et al., 2013]; 1:5000; rabbit anti-OLLAS 1:1000 [GenScript, A01658]; guinea pig anti-SUN-1 S8P, 1:700 [Woglar et al., 2013]) were added and incubated overnight in a humid chamber with a parafilm cover. Slides were then washed three times in PBST for 10 min each and incubated with secondary antibodies (goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 488, Thermo Fisher, Cat# A11034; goat anti-chicken Alexa Fluor488, Thermo Fisher, Cat# A11039; goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 555, Thermo Fisher, Cat# A21428; GFP booster, Chromotek, gb2AF488-50; goat anti-guinea pig Alex Fluor 488, Thermo Fisher, Cat# A11073) at 1:200 dilution for 2 hr in a humid chamber with a parafilm cover. Slides were washed two times in PBST then incubated with 2 µg/mL DAPI for 15–20 min in a humid chamber. Prior to mounting, slides were washed once more in PBST for 10 min and mounted using Vectashield with a 22 × 22 mm coverslip (no. 1.5). Slides were sealed with nail polish and stored at 4°C until imaged. GFP::MSH-5 slides were imaged within 24–48 hr of mounting due to significant signal loss in the GFP::MSH-5 staining if the slide were stored longer.

### Image analysis and quantification

#### FRAP quantification

The quantification of fluorescence recovery of GFP::SYP-2 and mCherry::SYP-3 was determined using FIJI. All photobleaching movies were first stabilized using the FIJI plugin ‘StackRegJ’ (https://research.stowers.org/imagejplugins/) to reduce the nuclear and worm motion in the germline. Photobleached nuclei were cropped to exclude as much extra z volume outside the size of the nucleus as possible. Then, these nuclei were sum intensity z-projected and the fluorescence intensity of the photobleached region was monitored using the rectangle tool. A small box was drawn on the segment of SC that will be photobleached, and through each frame of the timelapse the fluorescence intensity was recorded to obtain pre-bleach, bleach, and post-bleach fluorescence intensity values for a total of 35 min. Similar to Pattabiraman et al., 2017, we also excluded any nucleus that rotated or shifted in such a way that the photobleached SC segment could not be tracked between frames of the timelapse.

Nuclei in early pachytene were defined by being within the first 5–6 rows of pachytene, and nuclei in late pachytene were defined by being within the last 5–6 rows of pachytene. Mid pachytene nuclei were selected by being located within the middle region of pachytene. At each of these regions, the fluorescent intensity of three background regions of interest was determined per germline and averaged together to give the average background intensity. The average background intensity was subtracted from the fluorescence intensity of the photobleached SC segment. Additionally, the FRAP data from each SC segment was normalized such that the segment intensity pre-photobleach was 1 and the intensity immediately post-photobleached was 0. This allows us to determine the fraction of fluorescence intensity of each SYP protein that recovered following 35 min post-photobleaching. For oocytes, 3–5 germlines were used for GFP::SYP-2 and mCherry::SYP-3 analysis. For spermatocytes 3–6, germlines were used for GFP::SYP-2 and mCherry::SYP-3 analysis. For both sexes, 8–11 nuclei were analyzed in each region of pachytene and the specific n values in each region are reported in the figure legend. All images have been sum intensity projected and slightly adjusted for brightness and contrast. Additionally, any brightness and contrast adjustments made to oocyte images were also applied to spermatocyte images.

#### SC intensity quantification

The quantification of GFP::SYP-2, mCherry::SYP-3, SYP-5::GFP, and SYP-6::GFP was performed using Imaris (Oxford Instruments) in combination with our whole gonad analysis, described in Toraason et al., 2021. The assembled, chromatin-associated SYP signal in each nucleus was surfaced in Imaris to obtain the sum intensity and volume of the assembled. The start of pachytene was defined by the first row that did not contain more the 1–2 nuclei of transition zone nuclei (nuclei with DNA in a polarized or ‘crescent’-shaped morphology) and full-length SC. We assessed nuclei shape using both the nuclear fluorescent haze produced by unassembled fluorescently tagged SYPs and the assembled chromatin-associated SC. The end of pachytene was defined by the last row that contained all pachytene nuclei with the occasional single diplotene nucleus. The pachytene region was then equally divided into three zones based on the length of this region within the germline to generate early pachytene, mid pachytene, and late pachytene. These criteria were used for establishing the early pachytene, mid pachytene, and late pachytene in both hermaphrodite and male germlines. Nuclei were excluded from the analysis if they were not in a single layer on the bottom half of the imaged germline rachis due to an intensity decrease caused by higher amounts of light scatter from being deeper in germline.

Our whole gonad analysis was used to align GFP::SYP-2, mCherry::SYP-3, SYP-5::GFP, and SYP-6::GFP surfaced nuclei along the germline length (Toraason et al., 2021). Each nucleus was then normalized by its volume to determine the normalized sum intensity of each nucleus during pachytene. The length of pachytene was also normalized per germline from 0 (early pachytene) to 1 (late pachytene). Since SYP-6 disassembles in oocytes prior to the end of pachytene, SYP-6::GFP was normalized to the SYP-6::GFP distance, which was measured from early pachytene (0) to the end of the SYP-6::GFP signal (1) for each germline. To calculate the average and standard deviation of the normalized SYP intensity of each nucleus during pachytene, we binned the data using a sliding window of 0.01. Also, 7–12 germlines were analyzed for all genotypes and both sexes. During the course of this study, we discovered that all images from May 2022 up to September 2022 needed to be corrected for a 15% drop in the power of the 561 nm laser. This correction was applied to the sum intensity of mCherry::SYP-3 for all genotypes imaged during this time period, which included spo-11 oocytes and spermatocytes, syp-2/+ oocytes and spermatocytes, cosa-1 spermatocytes, syp-3/+ oocytes and spermatocytes, and wild-type oocytes and spermatocytes. The number of nuclei analyzed within early, mid, and late pachytene in each genotype is reported in as source data for Figures 2, 3, 7 and 8. All images have been sum intensity projected and slightly adjusted for brightness and contrast with the same settings between mutants and sexes.

#### SC length quantification

SC length measurements were determined on deconvolved DeltaVision images in Imaris using the filament tracer tool. Each chromosome within a nucleus was traced following the SYP-1 signal. If all six chromosomes could not be traced, then that nucleus was excluded from the analysis. Nuclei in early pachytene were defined by being within the first 5–6 rows of pachytene, and nuclei in late pachytene were defined by being within the last 5–6 rows of pachytene. Mid pachytene nuclei were selected by being located within the middle region of pachytene. For spermatocyte nuclei with six SC tracks, the smallest trace length was removed from the analysis because we inferred it to be the hemizygous X chromosome inappropriately assembled in the SC (Jaramillo-Lambert and Engebrecht, 2010). For oocytes, 10 nuclei in early pachytene were traced, 10 nuclei in mid pachytene were traced, and 12 nuclei in late pachytene were traced. For spermatocytes, 11 nuclei in early pachytene were traced, 12 nuclei in mid pachytene were traced, and 13 nuclei in late pachytene were traced.

#### Germline measurement quantifications of transition zone, DSB-2 staining, SUN-1 S8P, and SYP-1 assembly

Germline measurement quantification was performed using Imaris in combination with our whole gonad analysis protocol, described in Toraason et al., 2021. Imaged gonads were stitched together using the FIJI (NIH) plugin Stitcher (Preibisch et al., 2009) and using the measurement tool in Imaris. The positions of points along the germline were recorded by marking specific regions indicating the start of the germline at the pre-meiotic tip, start of the transition zone, start of DSB-2 staining, start of SUN-1 S8P, start of SYP-1 assembly, end of transition zone, end of DSB-2 zone, end of SUN-1 S8P, end of SYP-1 assembly, end of SYP-1 zone, end of pachytene, last nuclei with SUN-1 S8P, and end of straggler DSB-2 nuclei. DAPI morphology was used to determine the start and end of the transition and pachytene. From these recorded point positions, we calculated the length of (1) the transition zone, (2) SYP-1 assembly zone, (3) full-length SYP-1 zone, (4) SUN-1 S8P zone, (5) last nucleus with SUN-1 S8P zone, (6) DSB-2 zone, (7) DSB-2 straggler nuclei zone, and (8) pachytene. The start of the transition zone and pachytene was defined by the first row that did not contain more than 1–2 nuclei of either pre-meiotic nuclei (compact nuclei) or transition zone nuclei (nuclei with DNA in a polarized or ‘crescent’-shaped morphology), respectively. The end of pachytene was defined by the last row that contained all pachytene nuclei with the occasional single diplotene nucleus. The start of DSB-2 and SUN-1 S8P was determined by the position where the staining of each antibody began in a majority of the nuclei within a row, and the end of DSB-2 and SUN-1 S8P staining was determined by the position where the staining of each antibody was largely absent from a majority of the nuclei. The end of the DSB-2 straggler nuclei and SUN-1 S8P last nucleus was defined by the last nucleus in the germline with bright DSB-2 staining or SUN-1 S8P staining, respectively. The start of the SYP-1 assembly zone was defined by the germline position where small linear fragments of SYP-1 were observed, and the end of the SYP-1 assembly zone was defined by the germline position where all the nuclei in a row had full-length SYP-1 with only 1–2 discontinuities. The end of the SYP-1 zone was determined by the region where SYP-1 began to disassemble at the end of pachytene. The germline length was normalized per germline where 0 was the start of the germline at the pre-meiotic tip and 1 was the end of late pachytene. The number of germlines analyzed in each experiment is reported in the figure legends. All images have been max intensity projected and slightly adjusted for brightness and contrast.

#### RAD-51, MSH-5, and COSA-1 quantification

Imaged gonads were stitched together using the FIJI (NIH) plugin Stitcher (Preibisch et al., 2009) and analyzed in Imaris as described in Toraason et al., 2021 with minor changes. Each gonad from the start of pachytene through the end of pachytene was analyzed for RAD-51, MSH-5, or COSA-1 foci per nucleus, which was determined by DAPI morphology. The start of pachytene was defined by the first row that did not contain more than 1–2 nuclei of transition zone nuclei (nuclei with DNA in a polarized or ‘crescent’-shaped morphology). The end of pachytene was defined by the last row that contained all pachytene nuclei with the occasional single diplotene nucleus. The pachytene region was then equally divided into three zones based on the length of this region within the germline to generate early pachytene, mid pachytene, and late pachytene. The length of pachytene was also normalized per germline from 0 (early pachytene) to 1 (late pachytene). These criteria were used for establishing the early pachytene, mid pachytene, and late pachytene in both hermaphrodite and male germlines. For RAD-51, MSH-5, and COSA-1 foci per nucleus, sliding window averages and standard error of the mean (SEM) were calculated using a 0.01 bin size. Also, 7–12 germlines were analyzed for all genotypes and both sexes. The number of nuclei analyzed within early, mid, and late pachytene in each genotype is reported in the figure legends for each plot in Figure 5. All images have been max intensity projected and slightly adjusted for brightness and contrast.

### Western blot analysis

For both male and hermaphrodite, 100 adult worms were picked and washed once with M9 before being boiled for 5–10 min in sample buffer with occasional vortexing. For all western blots, samples were run on SDS-PAGE and wet transferred to low fluorescence PVDF membranes (Thermo Fisher Cat# 22860). Membranes were blocked in 5% milk in TBS + 0.1% Tween20 (TBST) for 1 hr at room temperature. Primary antibodies (anti-SYP-2 rabbit 1:1000 [gift from Yumi Kim], anti-Tubulin mouse 1:1000 [Abcam Cat# ab7291]) were incubated and agitated on an orbital shaker overnight at 4°C in 5% milk. Blots were washed three times for 10 min with TBST and LI-COR secondary antibodies (IRDye 680 donkey anti-mouse [LI-COR Cat# 926-68072], IRDye 800CW donkey anti-rabbit [LI-COR Cat# 926-32213]) were incubated at 1:1000 in TBST at room temperature for 1 hr. Blots were washed twice for 10 min each and imaged using LI-COR Odyssey Fc.

Since male worms only have one germline, all hermaphrodite samples were diluted to adjust for the two germlines present in hermaphrodite worms. To determine the correct dilution factor, we performed a dilution series of the hermaphrodite sample and measured the sum intensity of the SYP-2 bands in each dilution using FIJI (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). Then, we subtracted the background intensity from each SYP-2 measurement and normalized each dilution by the average intensity of SYP-2 from two undiluted male samples (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). From the normalized dilution curve, we determined that a 40% dilution of the hermaphrodite sample equated to similar amounts of SYP-2 in the undiluted male samples. This 40% dilution was applied to all hermaphrodite samples in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. To quantify the amount of SYP-2 in each sample, we used FIJI to measure the sum intensity of the SYP-2 and loading control alpha-tubulin bands that were both subtracted from a background intensity. Then, the background-subtracted SYP-2 intensity was normalized by the background-subtracted loading control alpha-tubulin intensity to generate a normalized SYP-2 intensity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

### Fertility assay

To assess hermaphrodite fertility, L4 hermaphrodite worms were placed onto new NGM plates and were transferred every 24 hr for a total of 2 d. To assess male fertility, single L4 male worms were mated to single L4 fog-2 obligate females and transferred every 24 hr for a total of 2 d before permanently removing the parental worms. After 3 d of removing the parental worms, each plate was scored for dead eggs. Then, the following day (4 d post removing parental worms) each plate was scored for living hermaphrodite and male progeny (male progeny was not scored in male fertility assays). Additionally, any progeny with mutant Unc or Dpy phenotypes was also scored for five worms in each genotype. Also, 7–10 worms were assayed for fertility for each genotype.

### SNP recombination mapping

SNP recombination mapping of chromosome II and X was performed as described in Bazan and Hillers, 2011 with minor changes. syp-2(ok307) and syp-3(ok785) were generated in Bristol (N2) backgrounds, and we PCR confirmed that both mutant strains carried all Bristol SNPs for both chromosomes assayed prior to mapping recombination. To generate Bristol/Hawaiian hybrids for mapping recombination, we crossed Bristol, syp-2(ok307) (DLW188), and syp-3(ok785) (DLW190) hermaphrodites to Hawaiian (CB4856) males. Then, 8–10 Bristol/Hawaiian hybrid L4 hermaphrodites were picked off the cross plates for oocyte recombination mapping and 10–15 Bristol/Hawaiian hybrid L4 males were picked off the cross plates for spermatocyte recombination. For oocyte recombination mapping, hybrid L4 hermaphrodites of each genotype were crossed to Bristol males, and male progeny were picked into 96-well plates for lysis and recombination PCR screening. For spermatocyte recombination mapping, hybrid L4 males of each genotype were crossed to Bristol hermaphrodites and male progeny were picked into 96-well plates for lysis and recombination PCR screening.

We used previously designed PCR primers and restriction digests to map six Bristol and Hawaiian SNPs on both chromosomes II and X (Bazan and Hillers, 2011). However, we were unable to get the primers to work for SNP E on chromosome II, so we redesigned new primers for this SNP that worked with the existing restriction digest for SNP identification at this genomic location. All SNP positions, PCR primers, restriction digests, and band sizes of the products for the Bristol or Hawaiian SNPs can be found in Supplementary file 2. The recombination frequency or map length in centiMorgans (cM) was calculated by taking the total number of crossovers identified in each interval divided by the total chromosomes scored multiplied by 100.

### Statistics

Statistical analysis of the FRAP data, SC length, SNP recombination mapping, and fertility assays was done using Prism. Mann–Whitney U tests adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni–Dunn method were performed on the FRAP data. Kruskal–Wallis tests were performed on the SC lengths with corrections for multiple comparisons. Chi-squared tests were performed on the entire SNP recombination mapping distribution. Pairwise comparisons between recombination intervals were performed using Fisher’s exact test. Chi-squared and Fisher’s exact tests were performed on the fertility assays. Mann–Whitney U tests adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni–Dunn method were performed on the SC intensity, quantification of RAD-51, MSH-5, and COSA-1, transition zone length, pachytene length, end of SYP-1 assembly zone, SUN-1 S8P zone, end of DSB-2 zone, and end of DSB-2 straggler zone using R. Each test used is indicated in the ‘Results’ section next to the reported p value, and all n values are reported in the figure legends.

Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Sexual dimorphic regulation of recombination by the synaptonemal complex" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Akira Shinohara as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Molly Przeworski as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

Based on reviews and discussions with reviewers, we do appreciate that your cytological and genetic analyses showing that two components of the central region of the synaptonemal complex (SC), SYP-2 and SYP-3, show sexually dimorphic dynamics and that the gene dosage of the two genes affects dynamics of SYP-2 and SYP-3 as well as dynamics and numbers of the recombination proteins, MSH-5 and COSA-1 distinctly in oocytes and spermatocytes. However, we are very sorry that we are not positive about the publication of the current version of the paper. Your paper is very descriptive and does not provide molecular insights into how oocytes and spermatocytes control the two SC components, SYP-2 and SYP-3 differentially and also how the gene dosage of the two components affects the dynamics of themselves as well as the recombination proteins.

To strengthen the conclusion of the paper, we asked you to address the following major points as well as comments from each reviewer. If you do not agree with our comments, please feel free to rebut them.

1. In this paper, the dynamics of SYP-2 and SYP-3, have been described. A previous study by Dernburg and her colleagues showed that the central region of the SC has liquid crystalline properties (eLife, 2017) by analyzing SYP-2 dynamics. In this regard, the different behaviour of SYP-3 looks interesting given that the two components are in the same compartment within a liquid crystalline matrix. It would be very nice to show/confirm the other components of the SC central region such as SYP-1, SYP-4, and SYP-5/6. As an extension, it would be nice to examine the haplo-inefficiency of SYP-2 and/or SYP-3 on the dynamics of the aforementioned SC components. Do those other SC components also display haploinsufficiency? This could at least be addressed with basic assays.

2. To address the sexual dimorphic properties of SYP-2 and SYP-3, it is very important to check the amount of proteins in both oocytes and spermatocytes. And if possible, it would be great to address the difference in post-translational modifications between the two sexes.

3. The authors used different tags (GFP for SYP-2 and mCherry for SYP-3) in the FRAP experiments. In the strict sense, it would be better to use the same tag for the analysis of dynamics. At least the authors have to show the different tags do not affect the dynamics of the proteins in gonads by experiments (or citing the paper).

4. It is important to re-write the text in a more concise way including shortening the Introduction part. Rather than mentioning P-values in the text, it would be nice to put these values in a different (supplemental) table or put it in the legend.

results.result: C. elegans germlines are organized as spatial-temporal gradients in both sexes, with the SC assembling late in the transition zone and becoming fully assembled by pachytene. Six SYP proteins (SYP-1–SYP-6) span the gap between homologous chromosomes in the SC.

results.result: SYP-2 and SYP-3 exhibit sex-specific differences in protein turnover dynamics within the SC during pachytene, with SYP-2 being more dynamic in spermatocytes and SYP-3 more dynamic in oocytes during early pachytene. Both sexes show progressive stabilization throughout pachytene, but SYP-2 and SYP-3 can be independently regulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C5–C12 are supported by FRAP data presented in Figure 1C and supplementary figures, with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni–Dunn adjusted Mann–Whitney tests). The data demonstrate sex-specific differences in protein dynamics and independent regulation of SYP-2 and SYP-3, with appropriate controls and replication.

results.result: SC length is similar throughout pachytene in each sex, with slightly shorter SC lengths in late pachytene spermatocytes likely due to differences in chromosome compaction. Independent regulation of SYP-2 and SYP-3 is not due to changes in chromosome length.
results.evaluation: Claims C13–C15 are supported by SC length measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, with appropriate statistical analysis. The conclusion that independent SYP regulation is not due to chromosome length changes is a reasonable inference from the data showing similar SC lengths between sexes.

results.result: The accumulation of GFP::SYP-2 in the SC is sexually dimorphic. Wild-type oocytes progressively accumulate SYP-2 until early/mid pachytene transition then maintain constant levels, while spermatocytes progressively load SYP-2 until late pachytene. Early pachytene spermatocytes have less SYP-2 than oocytes, but late pachytene spermatocytes have near or slightly more SYP-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C16–C21 are supported by quantitative fluorescence intensity data in Figure 2A and B with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney). The data include quantitative measurements with standard deviations and appropriate sample sizes (7–12 germlines analyzed).

results.result: mCherry::SYP-3 progressively accumulates throughout pachytene in both sexes, with spermatocytes incorporating less SYP-3 than oocytes. Fluorescent tag differences do not largely influence SYP-3 incorporation. Bright SYP-2 nuclei may have defects that only trigger a response with SYP-2 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C22–C27 are supported by data in Figure 2C and D with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney) and comparison to prior work using GFP::SYP-3 (Pattabiraman et al., 2017). The inference about bright SYP-2 nuclei (C26) is reasonable based on the observation that bright SYP-3 nuclei were not observed.

results.result: In C. elegans, SPO-11-induced DSBs are formed in the context of fully assembled SC in early pachytene and are repaired as nuclei traverse through pachytene. By late pachytene, crossover events are designated and marked by COSA-1. The SC is modified in response to recombination and alterations of the SC influence recombination in oocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C28–C30 are well-established facts from prior work, supported by multiple citations (Gartner and Engebrecht, 2022; Yokoo et al., 2012; Almanzar et al., 2023; Cahoon et al., 2019; and others). These provide essential background for the study.

results.result: In spo-11 mutants, both GFP::SYP-2 and mCherry::SYP-3 levels are significantly increased in oocytes but not spermatocytes. Western blot analysis shows a slight, non-significant increase in SYP-2 protein levels in oocytes only. The incorporation of SYPs is regulated in a recombination-dependent and sex-specific manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C31–C37 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 3A and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The sex-specific response to loss of DSBs is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical analysis and controls.

results.result: cosa-1 oocytes show different patterns of SYP-2 and SYP-3 accumulation compared to spo-11 oocytes, with an initial decrease in early pachytene followed by increases in mid and late pachytene. cosa-1 spermatocytes do not largely alter SYP-2 and SYP-3 levels. SYP levels in oocytes can be differentially regulated depending on the specific recombination stage impeded.
results.evaluation: Claims C38–C43 are supported by data in Figure 3B and D with quantitative fold-change measurements. The comparison between spo-11 and cosa-1 mutants demonstrates that SYP regulation depends on the specific stage of recombination that is disrupted, with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

results.result: Reducing the dosage of SYP-1, SYP-2, or SYP-3 by 60–70% permits SC assembly and crossover designation in oocytes. The transition zone is not significantly extended in syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ mutants in either sex, indicating chromosome pairing is not impaired.
results.evaluation: Claims C44–C45 are supported by prior work (Libuda et al., 2013) and data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The transition zone measurements with DAPI morphology provide appropriate evidence that chromosome pairing is not impaired by SYP dosage reduction.

results.result: SC assembly and/or maintenance are altered by reducing SYP-2 dosage only in oocytes. syp-2/+ oocytes display more SC discontinuities in early pachytene and a significantly increased SC assembly zone length, but maintain full-length SC after this zone. syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ spermatocytes show no significant SC assembly defects. The defect is not severe enough to trigger synapsis checkpoint activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C46–C52 are supported by SYP-1 staining data in Figure 4 with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney) and SUN-1 S8 phosphorylation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The sex-specific effect of SYP-2 dosage on SC assembly is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls.

results.result: The number and timing of RAD-51 foci per nucleus during pachytene differ between sexes, with oocytes initiating DSBs later than spermatocytes. Altering SYP dosage does not have large effects on DSB initiation or repair progression in either sex, though slight changes in RAD-51 foci were noted in syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ oocytes during early pachytene.
results.evaluation: Claims C53–C58 are supported by RAD-51 foci quantification in Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and DSB-2 staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The data show that while there are sex-specific differences in RAD-51 dynamics, SYP dosage does not largely impact DSB formation and repair, with appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: Wild-type spermatocytes reach peak MSH-5 foci earlier than oocytes and have higher peak amounts. Reducing SYP-2 or SYP-3 dosage causes significant changes in MSH-5 foci in oocytes. syp-2/+ oocytes show reduced MSH-5 foci throughout pachytene, while syp-3/+ oocytes show increased MSH-5 foci in early/mid pachytene followed by rapid loss. SYP-3 dosage regulates the timing of MSH-5 loading and off-loading in oocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59–C65 are supported by MSH-5 foci quantification in Figure 5C with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney). The data clearly demonstrate sex-specific and SYP-specific effects on MSH-5 dynamics, with appropriate controls and sample sizes (7–12 germlines).

results.result: In spermatocytes, only reducing SYP-2 dosage causes significant changes in MSH-5 foci. syp-2/+ spermatocytes initially form wild-type levels of MSH-5 foci but rapidly lose them during mid and late pachytene. SYP-2 dosage is important for MSH-5 stability in both sexes, while SYP-3 dosage does not change MSH-5 foci in spermatocytes, illustrating a sex-specific role for SYP-3.
results.evaluation: Claims C66–C70 are supported by MSH-5 foci quantification in Figure 5D with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney). The data demonstrate both conserved (SYP-2) and sex-specific (SYP-3) roles in regulating MSH-5 at DSB sites.

results.result: Both sexes load COSA-1 in mid pachytene, establishing 6 foci in oocytes and 5–6 foci in spermatocytes by late pachytene. Altering SYP-2 or SYP-3 dosage changes the timing of COSA-1 loading in both sexes, with earlier loading in syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ oocytes and delayed loading in syp-3/+ spermatocytes. The final number of COSA-1 foci is not changed, and six DAPI bodies are observed at diakinesis in syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ oocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C71–C78 are supported by COSA-1 foci quantification in Figure 5E and F with statistical analysis (p<0.001 or p<0.05, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney) and diakinesis observations (30/30 oocytes with six DAPI bodies for both mutants). The data demonstrate that SYP dosage regulates the timing but not the final number of crossover designations.

results.result: On chromosome II, both syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ alter the crossover landscape only in oocytes, with no significant changes in spermatocytes. Both mutants increase crossing over in the first interval (A to B) by ~10 cM, which is where the pairing center is located. This suggests crossovers are more often formed where the SC is first assembled at the pairing center when SYP dosage is reduced.
results.evaluation: Claims C79–C84 are supported by SNP recombination mapping data in Figure 6 and Table 1 with statistical analysis (chi-squared and Fisher's exact tests). The sex-specific effect on crossover distribution is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanistic explanation (C84) is presented as a possible explanation with supporting citations.

results.result: syp-2/+ oocytes show a significant decrease in crossover frequency on the X chromosome (51 cM to 32 cM), while syp-3/+ oocytes show no significant changes. Despite the large decrease in crossing over, syp-2/+ does not display elevated male progeny or increased dead eggs in either Bristol or Bristol/Hawaiian hybrid backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C85–C88 are supported by SNP mapping data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis. However, the lack of increased male progeny or dead eggs despite a significant reduction in X chromosome recombination is puzzling and unexplained. The authors acknowledge this discrepancy but do not provide a satisfactory explanation, suggesting additional work is needed to understand this phenotype.

results.result: syp-3/+ hermaphrodites exhibit increased lethality (dead eggs) and higher incidence of male progeny compared to wild-type in both Bristol and hybrid backgrounds. syp-3/+ also produces a higher rate of progeny with dumpy and/or uncoordinated mutant phenotypes. These phenotypes are likely due to error-prone repair using nonhomologous end joining. Spermatocyte fertility is unaffected in syp-2/+ or syp-3/+.
results.evaluation: Claims C89–C94 are supported by fertility data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis (chi-squared and Fisher's exact tests). The inference about error-prone repair (C91) is supported by citations to prior work showing SYP proteins regulate DSB repair pathway choice and that syp-3 nulls use nonhomologous end joining. The sex-specific effects on fertility are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Altering syp-2 gene dosage results in both sexes initially having an ~0.7-fold decrease in SYP-2 amounts within the SC, but SYP-2 levels progressively increase throughout pachytene until wild-type amounts are reached or pachytene ends. Western blot analysis shows GFP::SYP-2 protein levels are not significantly increased in syp-2/+ oocytes and spermatocytes. Both sexes attempt to compensate for haploinsufficiency by loading as much SYP-2 into the SC as possible.
results.evaluation: Claims C95–C97 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 7A and western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The data demonstrate that both sexes respond similarly to reduced syp-2 gene dosage by progressively increasing SYP-2 incorporation into the SC, despite no significant increase in total protein levels.

results.result: SYP-3 accumulation in syp-2/+ mutants displays sex-specific responses. In oocytes, reducing syp-2 gene dosage results in decreased SYP-3 levels that become more pronounced in late pachytene. In spermatocytes, reducing syp-2 gene dosage results in increased SYP-3 amounts in early pachytene that are indistinguishable from wild-type by late pachytene. SYP-3 levels within assembled SC are inversely affected via sex-specific mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C98–C101 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 7B with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney). The data clearly demonstrate sex-specific responses of SYP-3 to reduced syp-2 gene dosage, with opposite effects in oocytes versus spermatocytes.

results.result: Altering syp-3 gene dosage results in the same overall changes to SYP-2 and SYP-3 amounts in each sex as altering syp-2 gene dosage, though the degree of change differs. Reducing syp-3 gene dosage causes an initial reduction in SYP-2 levels in both sexes that is less than in syp-2/+, but both sexes progressively increase SYP-2 amounts until wild-type levels are reached. Western blot analysis shows both sexes only slightly increase SYP-2 protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C102–C106 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 7A and C and western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The data demonstrate that both sexes respond to alterations in syp gene dosages with similar trends of SYP-2 accumulation within the SC, with quantitative fold-change measurements provided.

results.result: In oocytes, reducing syp-3 gene dosage causes a stronger decrease in SYP-3 amounts compared to syp-2/+. In spermatocytes, syp-3/+ displays an increase in SYP-3 levels similar to syp-2/+ spermatocytes. The dosage of each SYP gene influences SYP-2 and SYP-3 accumulation similarly for each sex. Oocytes respond by decreasing both SYP-2 and SYP-3, while spermatocytes respond by decreasing SYP-2 and increasing SYP-3.
results.evaluation: Claims C107–C111 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 7B and D with quantitative fold-change measurements. The data clearly demonstrate sex-specific responses to reduced syp gene dosage, with oocytes and spermatocytes showing opposite patterns of SYP-3 regulation.

results.result: The composition of SYP-5 within the SC is sexually dimorphic. In wild-type oocytes, SYP-5::GFP accumulation progressively increases throughout pachytene. Wild-type spermatocytes also show progressive increase but with significantly less total SYP-5::GFP than oocytes, especially in late pachytene where oocytes have 1.8-fold more SYP-5. The accumulation patterns of SYP-3 and SYP-5 are very similar.
results.evaluation: Claims C112–C116 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 8A with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney) and comparison to prior work (Hurlock et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). The quantitative fold-change measurement (1.8-fold) is provided for the sex-specific difference in late pachytene.

results.result: In syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ oocytes, SYP-5::GFP accumulation significantly decreases throughout pachytene, the same response as SYP-3 levels. In spermatocytes, syp-2/+ does not influence SYP-5::GFP amounts, but syp-3/+ significantly decreases SYP-5::GFP accumulation. This suggests SYP-5 and SYP-3 may be regulated similarly in oocyte SC but differentially in spermatocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C117–C120 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 8A comparing responses to syp-2/+ and syp-3/+ in both sexes. The data demonstrate sex-specific regulation of SYP-5 in response to altered SYP dosage, with appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: SYP-6 is the paralog of SYP-5 with some functional redundancy in SC assembly in oocytes. Both are assembled into the SC in the same region but disassembled at different times. In oocytes, SYP-5 is disassembled in diplotene while SYP-6 is disassembled in mid pachytene. Unlike oocytes, SYP-6 persists in spermatocytes through late pachytene and disassembles in diplotene with other SYPs. SYP-5 localization is identical in each sex. The retention of SYP-6 in late pachytene indicates sexually dimorphic SC composition.
results.evaluation: Claims C121–C126 are supported by prior work (Hurlock et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020) and new data in Figure 8B and C showing SYP-6 localization in spermatocytes. This is a novel finding demonstrating sex-specific differences in SYP-6 disassembly timing, with appropriate imaging and controls.

results.result: SYP-6 has a different incorporation pattern than SYP-5 in oocytes. In wild-type oocytes, SYP-6::GFP remains at a fairly constant amount before disassembly in mid pachytene. Unlike SYP-5, syp-2 and syp-3 gene dosage does not have a strong effect on SYP-6::GFP amounts in oocytes. SYP-5 and SYP-6 within oocyte SC are differentially regulated, suggesting non-redundant roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C127–C130 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 8D comparing SYP-6 and SYP-5 patterns and responses to altered SYP dosage. The differential regulation is clearly demonstrated, supporting the inference of non-redundant roles, with citation to prior work (Zhang et al., 2020).

results.result: In early pachytene, both wild-type oocytes and spermatocytes display similar amounts of SYP-6::GFP. By mid pachytene, while oocytes disassemble SYP-6, spermatocytes only show a slight reduction. Altering SYP-2 dosage influences SYP-6::GFP incorporation in spermatocyte SC. syp-2/+ spermatocytes display a significant increase in SYP-6::GFP incorporation throughout pachytene.
results.evaluation: Claims C131–C134 are supported by fluorescence intensity data in Figure 8D and E with statistical analysis (p<0.001, Bonferroni adjusted Mann–Whitney). The data demonstrate sex-specific regulation of SYP-6 in response to altered SYP-2 dosage, with spermatocytes showing increased SYP-6 incorporation.

results.result: The regulation of SYP-2, SYP-3, SYP-5, and SYP-6 is different in spermatocytes and oocytes, suggesting sex-specific roles for each protein during meiosis. Altering SYP-2 and SYP-3 dosage causes global, sexually dimorphic changes within the SC that are likely a response to and/or consequence of defects in specific steps of recombination.
results.evaluation: Claims C136–C137 are supported by the comprehensive data on SYP regulation presented in Figures 7 and 8. The conclusion that regulation is sex-specific and linked to recombination defects is a reasonable synthesis of the multiple lines of evidence presented throughout the study.

results.result: The SC in C. elegans regulates recombination via sexually dimorphic mechanisms. SYP-2 and SYP-3 have sex-specific differences in protein turnover rates that may influence sexually dimorphic SC composition. SYP-2, SYP-3, SYP-5, and SYP-6 are incorporated at different levels via sex-specific mechanisms. SYP protein levels in the SC are dependent on recombination and SYP protein dosage impacts recombination regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C138–C141 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the comprehensive data on SYP dynamics (Figure 1), composition (Figures 2, 7, 8), recombination dependence (Figure 3), and effects on recombination (Figures 5, 6). These conclusions are well-supported by multiple independent lines of evidence.

results.result: The amount of SYP-2 within the SC of oocytes promotes the formation and/or maintenance of joint molecules. syp-2/+ oocytes incorporate less SYP-2 during stages when MSH-5-stabilized joint molecules are formed and exhibit severe reduction in MSH-5 foci. This relationship is SYP-2 specific, as reduced SYP-3 levels do not result in reduced MSH-5 foci. A specific threshold of SYP-2 ensures joint molecule formation and/or stabilization.
results.evaluation: Claims C142–C145 are supported by data in Figures 5 and 7 showing the correlation between reduced SYP-2 levels and reduced MSH-5 foci in oocytes, and the lack of this effect with reduced SYP-3. The threshold model is a reasonable interpretation of the data, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Spermatocyte SYP-2 dosage is required for maintenance of MSH-5-marked joint molecules. Reducing SYP-2 levels in spermatocytes does not alter SC assembly, allowing initial formation of wild-type MSH-5 foci levels, but rapid loss during mid pachytene suggests destabilization rather than rapid resolution. This function appears conserved between sexes, but the specific threshold of SYP-2 required is significantly reduced in spermatocytes compared to oocytes, suggesting mechanistic differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C146–C152 are supported by data in Figures 4 and 5 showing normal SC assembly but altered MSH-5 dynamics in syp-2/+ spermatocytes, and comparison to oocytes in Figures 2, 5, and 7. The model favoring destabilization over rapid resolution is reasonable given the lack of premature COSA-1 loading.

results.result: SYP-3 dosage in oocytes regulates the timing of recombination steps. SYP-3 accumulates throughout pachytene as recombination intermediates are processed. When SYP-3 levels are reduced, MSH-5-marked joint molecules and COSA-1-marked crossover designation appear prematurely, coinciding with disproportionate crossover formation near the pairing center on chromosome II. This phenotype is likely underpinned by SYP-3 levels as it is also present in syp-2/+. The timing of recombination events appears sensitive to SYP-3 amounts.
results.evaluation: Claims C153–C160 are supported by data in Figures 2, 5, 6, and 7 showing the correlation between reduced SYP-3 levels, premature recombination events, and altered crossover positioning. The inference that the phenotype in syp-2/+ is due to reduced SYP-3 levels is reasonable given the data in Figure 7 showing reduced SYP-3 in syp-2/+ oocytes.

results.result: In spermatocytes, SYP-3 also regulates the timing of recombination events. However, spermatocytes' SYP-3 incorporation is minimally impacted by syp-3/+ heterozygosity, explaining the absence of crossover positioning defects. SYP-3 levels are subtly elevated in early pachytene in syp-3/+ spermatocytes, coinciding with a delay in crossover designation. Titrating SYP-3 incorporation may regulate the timing of recombination events between sexes given different timescales of spermatogenesis and oogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C161–C165 are supported by data in Figures 5, 6, and 7 showing the relationship between SYP-3 levels and recombination timing in spermatocytes. The suggestion that SYP-3 titration may regulate timing between sexes (C165) is a reasonable speculation supported by citation to prior work on timing differences (Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2007).

results.result: The SC in C. elegans is sexually dimorphic. Sex-specific differences in SYP-2 and SYP-3 dynamics suggest differences in protein regulation between sexes. Progressive stabilization of SC in oocytes has been linked to phosphorylation of SYP proteins. Many SYP proteins are post-translationally modified in response to recombination in oocytes. Since spermatocytes show similar progressive stabilization, the same post-translational modifications may have similar functions in spermatocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C166–C170 are supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to prior work on post-translational modifications (Nadarajan et al., 2017; Pattabiraman et al., 2017; Garcia-Muse et al., 2019; others). The speculation about similar modifications in spermatocytes (C170) is reasonable given the similar stabilization patterns observed.

results.result: SYP-2 is more dynamic in spermatocytes even in the 'stabilized' state in late pachytene, suggesting spermatocytes may not stabilize the SC to the same degree as oocytes. One reason could be to allow DSBs in late pachytene to be repaired with the homolog. In oocytes, SC stabilization in late pachytene prevents formation of more crossovers. Spermatocytes have differences in DNA repair, crossover numbers, and checkpoints that may require a more dynamic SC.
results.evaluation: Claims C171–C175 are supported by FRAP data in Figure 1 and citations to prior work on sex-specific differences in DNA repair and checkpoints (Checchi et al., 2014; Gabdank and Fire, 2014; others). The speculation about reasons for increased dynamics (C173) is reasonable given the known differences between sexes.

results.result: The amount of SYP-2, SYP-3, and SYP-5 required for proper recombination execution is significantly different between oocytes and spermatocytes. Oocytes require more of these proteins during early and mid pachytene. SYP-2 levels in spermatocytes reach oocyte levels in late pachytene, and SYP-6 levels are nearly identical in early pachytene. Spermatocytes have increased SYP-2 turnover dynamics in late pachytene, which may facilitate DSB repair since spermatocytes do not undergo checkpoint-mediated apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C176–C180 are supported by data in Figures 1, 2, 8, and 9 showing sex-specific differences in SYP amounts and dynamics. The inference about facilitating DSB repair (C179) is reasonable given the citation to prior work showing spermatocytes lack checkpoint-mediated apoptosis (Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2010).

results.result: Reduced SYP-3 dosage triggers an increase in SYP-3 composition within the SC, suggesting spermatocytes may compensate for loss of a functional syp-3 copy. One way spermatocytes could alter SYP-3 levels is to alter SYP-3 turnover rates within the SC. Spermatocytes have altered protein dynamics in the SC compared to oocytes. Sex-specific differences in SYP-2 and SYP-3 dynamics may regulate SC composition during pachytene.
results.evaluation: Claims C181–C184 are supported by data in Figures 1 and 7 showing increased SYP-3 in syp-3/+ spermatocytes and sex-specific differences in dynamics. The speculation about altering turnover rates (C182) is reasonable given the demonstrated differences in dynamics.

results.result: In nearly all SC-containing organisms, central region proteins are dependent on each other for SC assembly. In C. elegans, SYP proteins are also dependent on each other for protein stability, leading to the assumption of complete interdependence. However, fluctuations in SYP-2 and SYP-3 levels can differentially influence amounts of each other and other SYPs, and each SYP can be regulated independently. These differences in SYP-2 and SYP-3 proportions are directly involved in regulating specific recombination steps.
results.evaluation: Claims C185–C189 are supported by prior work (Cahoon and Hawley, 2016; Colaiácovo et al., 2003) and data in Figures 2, 3, 7, and 8 demonstrating independent regulation of SYPs. This challenges the previous assumption of complete interdependence and is a significant conceptual advance.

results.result: Some SYPs display similar accumulation patterns and respond similarly to changes in SYP protein levels, such as SYP-5 and SYP-3 in oocytes. Each SYP in the SC maintains both SYP-dependent functions (e.g., assembling the SC) and SYP-independent functions (e.g., regulating specific recombination steps).
results.evaluation: Claims C190–C191 are supported by data in Figures 7 and 8 showing similar patterns for SYP-5 and SYP-3 in oocytes. The hypothesis of dual SYP-dependent and SYP-independent functions (C191) is a reasonable synthesis of the data showing both coordinated and independent regulation.

results.result: In worms and yeast, the SC grows in width throughout pachytene, suggesting dynamic protein composition. The incorporation of SYP-2 and SYP-3 is not proportional during pachytene. Recombination influences SYP accumulation patterns and each SYP is independently regulated within the SC. The ability to adjust SYP-2, SYP-3, SYP-5, and SYP-6 amounts demonstrates flexibility in SYP requirements for complex assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C192–C195 are supported by prior work (Pattabiraman et al., 2017; Voelkel-Meiman et al., 2012) and data in Figures 1, 3, 7, and 8. The conclusion about flexibility in SYP requirements is a reasonable interpretation of the data showing variable SYP amounts while maintaining SC assembly.

results.result: SYP-2 is positioned in the very center of the SC and may be slightly more external to SYP-3, SYP-5, and SYP-6, which would facilitate regulation of SYP-2 levels without compromising the complex. Proteins in the very central region play a critical role in recombination. These central proteins like SYP-2 may not have as strong structural roles as those positioned broadly in the central region like SYP-3.
results.evaluation: Claims C196–C198 are supported by prior work on SYP positioning (Köhler et al., 2020) and recombination roles (Gordon et al., 2021; Voelkel-Meiman et al., 2019, 2015, 2022). The inference about differential structural roles is reasonable given the data showing SYP-2 can be more readily adjusted without compromising SC assembly.

results.result: Sex-specific differences in SYP-6 localization and sexually dimorphic responses of SYP-5 and SYP-6 to SYP-2 and SYP-3 levels suggest individual sex-specific roles during meiosis. Null mutants indicate shared and distinct functions between SYP-5 and SYP-6. syp-5 mutants have stronger defects than syp-6 mutants, suggesting SYP-5 plays a more significant role in oocyte recombination. Sex-specific retention of SYP-6 in late pachytene spermatocytes suggests a spermatocyte-specific role. Retaining SYP-6 may facilitate repair of DSBs in late pachytene since spermatocytes lack checkpoint-mediated apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C199–C203 are supported by data in Figure 8 showing sex-specific SYP-6 localization and regulation, and citations to prior work (Hurlock et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2010). The speculation about facilitating DSB repair (C203) is reasonable given the known lack of checkpoint-mediated apoptosis in spermatocytes.

results.result: The patterns of SYP-2 and SYP-3 accumulation in the SC are different, and SYP dosage can influence amounts of other SYP proteins. Regardless of which SYP dosage is altered, the same change in SYP-2 and SYP-3 accumulation occurs individually for each sex. In oocytes, both SYP-2, SYP-3, and SYP-5 amounts decrease in response to reduced SYP-2 or SYP-3. In spermatocytes, reduced SYP-2 or SYP-3 decreases SYP-2, increases SYP-3, and does not change SYP-5. SYP-6 increases with reduced SYP-2 dosage but does not change with altered SYP-3 dosage. One explanation is that spermatocytes require a different stoichiometry of SC proteins compared to oocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C204–C210 are supported by comprehensive data in Figures 7 and 8 showing sex-specific patterns of SYP regulation in response to altered dosage. The speculation about different stoichiometry requirements (C209) is reasonable, with citation to prior work in mice showing structural differences in SC between sexes (Agostinho et al., 2018).
